                  REQUEST FOR REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION
                                   OF THE
                     INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS
           Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Rule 713 of the Rules of

Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),2 the

Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (“PJM Transmission Owners”)3 respectfully request

rehearing of the Commission’s June 18, 2026 order in this proceeding (“June 18 Order”).4

          As discussed below, the Commission should grant rehearing or provide clarification of the

June 18 Order, as follows:

           The Commission erred in concluding that co-located load and generation interconnected
            and synchronized with the transmission system should be exempt from any minimum
            charge, such as the Grid Reliance Charge proposed by the PJM Transmission Owners.
            The Commission failed to address the substantial evidence provided by the PJM
            Transmission Owners regarding the need for such a charge.

           The Commission erred by failing to address the substantial evidence provided by the PJM
            Transmission Owners regarding justness and reasonableness of the Grid Reliance Charge
            methodology for calculating such charge.

           The Commission erred in rejecting the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal to set the
            maximum rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service at the rate for Firm
            Contract Demand Service. The Commission failed to provide an adequate reason for
            rejecting PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal, in particular distinguishing the
            Commission’s precedent regarding non-firm point-to-point transmission service and
            addressing the PJM Transmission Owners’ explanation that further analysis and study
            regarding the use of these new services would be necessary before determining the

           define Co-Located Load based on facilities located on the customer’s side of the Point of
           Change of Ownership, rather than the Point of Interconnection. The Commission’s

          The Commission erred in rejecting PJM’s proposal to require Co-Located Load to take
           sufficient transmission service to cover its entire gross load. PJM’s proposal is a just and
           reasonable means to ensure that Co-Located Load can be served reliably and does not
           threaten the integrity of the transmission system.

          The Commission should clarify its ruling regarding the ability to require control

           PJM Transmission Owners will be permitted to require protection on both the customer
           and Transmission Owner sides of the Point of Interconnection, to the extent that a study
           determines that such protection is necessary and appropriate.

Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., pursuant to section 206 of the FPA, finding PJM’s Open Access

Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) unjust and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions

addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that

apply to generators serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service

        In the June 18 Order, the Commission addressed the requests for rehearing and clarification

of the December Order, PJM’s second compliance filing, and the paper hearing on the new

II.     REQUESTS FOR REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION

       B.       Arguments

                1.      The Commission Erred in Concluding That Co-Located Load and
                        Generation Interconnected and Synchronized With the Transmission
                        System Should be Exempt From any Minimum Charge, and Rejecting
                        the PJM Transmission Owners’ Proposed Grid Reliance Charge.

       In the June 18 Order, the Commission rejected the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed

Grid Reliance Charge, concluding that the record does not adequately substantiate the need for an

additional charge for co-located load at this time or how such a charge should be calculated and

assessed.12 The Commission indicated that it will consider such a charge after more experience

with the actual use of the new transmission services.13 The Commission should reverse this finding

on rehearing.

                        a.       A Minimum Charge Such as the Grid Reliance Charge is
                                 Necessary to Ensure That Co-Located Loads pay Their Fair
                                 Share of System Costs.

       The Grid Reliance Charge or some other minimum charge is a necessary component of the

new transmission services required under the Commission’s December Order.                The PJM



12
       June 18 Order at P 455.
13
       Id. at P 456.



                                                 7
 Transmission Owners developed the Grid Reliance Charge partially in response to Commissioner

Chang’s guidance that a just and reasonable replacement rate for the new transmission services

should reflect “some form of minimum transmission service charge, which would protect other

customers against cost shifts resulting from Co-Located Loads that rely upon the transmission

system but do not directly or meaningfully contribute to its costs via transmission service

payments.”14 The Grid Reliance Charge achieves this goal by reflecting the costs of using the

transmission system to deliver black start and regulation services, as well as the costs of providing

the inherent benefits that all customers, including Contract Demand customers, receive as a result

of their synchronization to and reliance on the grid.

        As the PJM Transmission Owners explained in their evidentiary submissions, even if a Co-

Located Load customer is not procuring transmission service for its entire on-site load, being

connected to the grid provides benefits in terms of the ability to access resources that are not co-

located with load if necessary, backing up co-located generation, and providing critical ancillary

services to Co-Located Load, such as regulation and black start. These grid benefits also include

delivering ancillary services and essential reliability services, such as frequency support, inertia,

voltage stability, fault current capability, ride-through and protection coordination, and providing

sufficient short-circuit capability.15 No party provided any evidence rebutting the nature of these

benefits.

        The purpose of a Grid Reliance Charge is not merely to recover the costs associated with

the delivery of ancillary services. Rather, its purpose is to ensure that Co-Located Load customers

24, 2026) (“Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer Rebuttal Testimony”).

interconnected customers, including essential reliability services, such as frequency support,

inertia, voltage stability, fault current capability, ride-through and protection coordination, and

sufficient short-circuit capability.16 Even if a Co-Located Load customer never “pulls energy from

the grid,” and only relies on black start and regulation service, it receives the inherent benefits that

come with grid interconnection, which requires transmission infrastructure, investment and

expense. A Grid Reliance Charge appropriately captures, with reasonable precision, the costs

associated with these inherent benefits by calculating the portions of annual depreciation and

operation and maintenance expenses that constitute a reasonable proxy for the costs of providing

those benefits.

        The June 18 Order fails to meaningfully consider and address these points. The only

rationale provided was that the record contains “insufficient description of the potential nature or

magnitude of the cited benefits or the potential costs that transmission providers or owners may

incur when providing these benefits to . . . Co-Located Loads.”17 The PJM Transmission Owners

disagree that the record is insufficient in this regard. At a minimum, Co-Located Load will utilize

the transmission system to receive black-start and regulation ancillary services, which the

Commission has already concluded are used by the entire on-site load of a Co-Located Load

facility.18 The Commission’s finding that Co-Located Load will receive the benefits of black-start

and regulation ancillary services cannot be squared with the rejection of a minimum charge such

as the Grid Reliance Charge. These findings amount to the unduly discriminatory, arbitrary, and

        In addition to providing black-start and regulation services, the PJM Transmission Owners

ultimately be borne by retail ratepayers.            Such a subsidy is unjust and unreasonable and

        The Commission’s commitment to consider a Grid Reliance Charge after more experience

with the actual use of the new transmission services21 is not sufficient. As discussed above, the

case for the Grid Reliance Charge is sound and the need for some minimum charge is imminent.

With the Commission’s goal of “speed to market” for Co-Located Loads, it is reasonable to expect

that customers will begin using the new transmission services that the Commission has required

as soon as feasible. Without a Grid Reliance Charge or other minimum charge to accompany the

implementation of these new services, Co-Located Load customers will enjoy the inherent benefits

of the PJM transmission system without providing any contribution to the costs of those benefits,

which is unduly preferential to Co-Located Load customers and unfair to the rest of customers

who will be responsible for bearing those costs.

                        b.       The Proposed Grid Reliance Charge Methodology is Just and
                                 Reasonable.

       In addition to granting rehearing on the need for a minimum charge in the first instance,

the Commission should also grant rehearing and find that the Grid Reliance Charge proposed by

the PJM Transmission Owners represents a just and reasonable methodology for implementing

such a charge. The Grid Reliance Charge is grounded in sound ratemaking and cost causation

principles. It represents an appropriate balance between fairly estimating the grid reliance benefits

to Co-Located Load and the need to ensure the rate can be practically implemented. Practicality

concerns are particularly pertinent here given the Commission’s desire to expedite the

interconnection of data center loads. This approach is also fully consistent with longstanding

Commission precedent holding that cost allocation rules do not require exacting precision as long

as they represent a comparison of the costs assessed to a party against the burdens imposed or



21
       June 18 Order at P 456.



                                                 11
 benefits drawn.22 The PJM Transmission Owner’s Grid Reliance Charge proposal meets this

standard.

        The PJM Transmission Owners provided substantial evidence supporting the calculation

of the Grid Reliance Charge, as set forth in expert witness testimony provided by Concentric

Energy Advisors.23 By including certain publicly-available costs and excluding others, the Grid

Reliance Charge methodology achieves the goal of developing a cost-based, transparent, and

practically implementable calculation.24 First, by intentionally limiting the Grid Reliance Charge

to specific depreciation and operations and maintenance accounts and excluding return on rate

base and associated income taxes, the Grid Reliance Charge methodology produces a conservative

result focused on allocating a reasonable share of those costs most directly related to the ongoing

operation and use of the grid, rather than investment return.25 Second, a Grid Reliance Charge

avoids the need to relitigate each utility’s rate base, return, or tax components and eliminates the

need for company-specific (or project-specific) engineering judgment and allocations.26 Third, by

establishing the Grid Reliance Charge as a percentage of the total transmission revenue

requirement, the Grid Reliance Charge scales proportionally with each utility’s size and cost

structure.27 Lastly, averaging the calculated Grid Reliance Charge percentages across all PJM

               2.       The Commission Erred in Rejecting the PJM Transmission Owners’
                        Proposal to set the Maximum Rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand
                        Transmission Service at the Rate for Firm Contract Demand
                        Transmission Service, Subject to Discount.

       In the June 18 Order, the Commission found that the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal

to set the maximum rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service equal to the rate for

Firm Contract Demand transmission service was not just and reasonable.29 In the Commission’s

view, Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is an inferior service to Firm Contract

Demand transmission service and NITS, making it unjust and unreasonable to charge Non-Firm

Contract Demand customers the same maximum rate as Firm Contract Demand and NITS

customers.30 The Commission should reverse this finding on rehearing.

       Contrary to the Commission’s conclusion, the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal is fully

consistent with Order No. 888, as embodied in the provisions of the Tariff addressing the

availability of firm and non-firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service. Rather, it is the June 18

Order that departs from Order No. 888 and related precedent. In Order No. 888, the Commission

rejected arguments that there is no cost-of-service principle justifying charging non-firm rates at

the same rate as firm service, making clear that it is important to allow pricing flexibility, and that

non-firm service can be priced at the same level of firm service under appropriate circumstances.31

       In the June 18 Order, the Commission rejected PJM’s proposal to require that the Eligible

Customer taking transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located Load must take sufficient

transmission service to account for the entire gross demand of the Co-Located Load.39 The

Commission determined that PJM’s proposal did not comply with the December Order and would

fundamentally alter the nature of Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission services.40 On rehearing, the Commission should reverse this finding.

       PJM proposes to require that the Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf

of a Co-Located Load must take sufficient transmission service to account for the entire gross

demand of the Co-Located Load. An Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of a Co-Located

Load must request Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service equal to the MW level of the

Co-Located Generator dedicated to serving the Co-Located Load. Any portion of the gross

demand of the Co-Located Load not served by the Co-Located Generator must be covered by Firm

Contract Demand transmission service. This arrangement would tie the amount of Firm Contract

Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission services that an Eligible Customer can

request to the size of the Co-Located Generator, rather than allowing the Eligible Customer to

select any amount, including 0 MW for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service.

       Requiring that an Eligible Customer on behalf of a Co-Located Load must take sufficient

transmission service to account for the entire gross demand of the Co-Located Load is just and

reasonable to ensure reliable operation of the transmission system.

        To ensure reliability, PJM’s studies examine the transmission service requests for the Co-

Located Load and the Co-Located Load’s impact on the transmission system. These studies must

capture the effects of any unscheduled energy withdrawals by the Co-Located Load, even if

inadvertent or limited in duration, and confirm that any such withdrawals will not jeopardize

which must be backed up by Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. Without this sort

including load taking service beyond levels for which PJM has properly studied and planned. A

and cascading outages.     The Commission’s disregard of those concerns was arbitrary and

capricious.

portion of the load not covered by Firm Contract Demand transmission service must be covered

                5.       The Commission Should Clarify its Ruling Regarding Requirements
                         for Control Technologies and Protection Systems.

        In the June 18 Order, the Commission rejected the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal

that the Tariff should specify that control technologies and/or protection systems may be required

on both the customer and PJM Transmission Owner sides of the Point of Interconnection.41 The

Commission held that the location and number of devices required should be based on engineering

judgment of PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners.42                 Consistent with this ruling, the

Commission should clarify that PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners will be permitted to

require protection on both the customer and Transmission Owner sides of the Point of

Interconnection, to the extent that a study determines that such protection is necessary and

appropriate.

        As a general matter, requiring control technologies and/or protection systems on both the

Co-Located Load customer’s and the PJM Transmission Owner’s side of the point of

interconnection provides much needed redundancy. On every other element of the bulk electric

system in PJM, there is an expectation for redundancy for protection systems that are primarily

responsible for fault clearing. In the case of Co-Located Load, the failure to adequately curtail

load or generation can adversely impact the transmission system just as significantly as a fault,

especially if there are no limitations on the size of the load and generation connected in one facility.

Without protection system redundancy, the transmission system and the millions of customers that

 rely on it will face significant risks that cannot be addressed effectively through operating

procedures, relaying, and remote tripping capability.

        Moreover, cost is not a meaningful barrier to implementing this level of redundancy. The

overall cost of implementing protection systems at a given facility is driven primarily by personnel

time for engineering, construction, and subsequent maintenance, rather than by significant material

costs. In any event, the benefits of requiring control technologies and/or protection systems on

both the Co-Located Load customer’s and the PJM Transmission Owner’s side of the point of

interconnection far outweigh the minimal cost of the protection system equipment, particularly

when compared to other costs associated with the development and interconnection of Co-Located

Load. Further, it is best to address system reliability concerns upfront before the Co-Located Load

first comes online because it is less expensive to install protection systems as part of initial

construction rather than retrofit the site after initial construction.

        For these reasons, if the Commission declines to clarify its ruling as stated above, it should

grant rehearing so as to allow PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners to require protection on

both the customer and PJM Transmission Owner sides of the Point of Interconnection when the

relevant study determines that such protection is necessary to provide adequate redundancy.
